clinicalPearls: An exceptionally rare inherited bleeding disorder caused by defective exposure of procoagulant phosphatidylserine on the activated platelet surface.
Most cases result from autosomal recessive mutations in ANO6 (TMEM16F), which encodes a calcium-activated phospholipid scramblase.
Platelet count, morphology and standard aggregation studies are normal, so routine coagulation and platelet testing are typically unremarkable.
Bleeding is characteristically deep and delayed after trauma or surgery, resembling a coagulation defect more than a typical platelet disorder.
The defect impairs assembly of tenase and prothrombinase complexes on the platelet membrane because the phosphatidylserine platform is not externalised.
Diagnosis relies on specialised assays showing reduced platelet-dependent thrombin generation and diminished annexin V binding by flow cytometry.
Failure of microparticle release and impaired factor Va/factor Xa binding are hallmark laboratory findings.
Management centres on antifibrinolytics and platelet transfusion for significant bleeding, since no specific replacement therapy exists.
reference.pathophysiology: Scott syndrome is caused by failure of the transmembrane phospholipid scrambling that normally follows platelet activation. In health, a rise in cytosolic calcium activates the scramblase encoded by ANO6 (TMEM16F), which collapses membrane phospholipid asymmetry and externalises phosphatidylserine on the outer leaflet of activated platelets, red cells and microparticles. This anionic surface is the essential catalytic platform for assembly of the tenase (factor VIIIa/IXa) and prothrombinase (factor Va/Xa) complexes that accelerate thrombin generation. In Scott syndrome, loss-of-function mutations abolish scramblase activity, so phosphatidylserine remains sequestered internally, microparticle formation is deficient and localised thrombin generation at the platelet surface is markedly impaired despite normal clotting factors and platelet aggregation. The result is a haemostatic defect that manifests chiefly after surgical or traumatic challenge.
additionalDifferentials: Platelet storage pool or secretion defects
Combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Flow-cytometric annexin V binding to activated platelets (decreased phosphatidylserine exposure)
Standard coagulation screen and platelet aggregometry (typically normal)
von Willebrand factor and coagulation factor assays to exclude alternatives
redFlags: Severe delayed haemorrhage following surgery, dental extraction or trauma
Bleeding disproportionate to normal routine coagulation and platelet tests
Large deep haematoma or intramuscular bleeding
Recurrent bleeding requiring repeated transfusion with alloimmunisation risk
reference.prognosis: With awareness of the diagnosis and appropriate peri-procedural haemostatic support the prognosis is good and spontaneous bleeding is uncommon. The main hazard is unanticipated severe bleeding during surgery or trauma when the disorder has not been recognised.
pitfalls: Excluding a bleeding disorder because routine coagulation and platelet function tests are normal.
Overlooking the need for specialised phosphatidylserine-exposure and thrombin-generation assays.
Assuming platelet transfusion alone always suffices without antifibrinolytic support.
Failing to plan haemostatic cover before elective surgery in a known patient.
Confusing the delayed deep bleeding pattern with a coagulation factor deficiency and misdirecting factor replacement.
references: International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis guidance on rare bleeding disorders
Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood, current edition
management: Provide platelet transfusion as the mainstay haemostatic cover for surgery, trauma, or significant bleeding, supplying a functional procoagulant platelet surface
Plan peri-procedural haemostatic support in advance, adding an antifibrinolytic such as tranexamic acid and considering recombinant activated factor VII for refractory bleeding
Avoid antiplatelet agents and other drugs that impair haemostasis
Ensure the rare diagnosis is documented and communicated, for example via an alert card, to anticipate deep, delayed bleeding
Confirm and monitor with specialised platelet-dependent thrombin generation and annexin V flow-cytometry assays
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive ANO6 (TMEM16F) disorder and refer to a haemostasis centre
